As outlined in FSAs own guidance, [ a ] Direct Consolidation Loan is treated as a single loan for purposes of forgiveness. Once 120 qualifying payments are made, the full remaining balance is forgiven ( StudentAid.gov PSLF FAQs ). Additionally, the IDR account adjustment rules confirm that [ b ] orrowers who consolidate will receive a weighted average of qualifying months from the underlying loans ( XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, 2022 ).

My StudentAid.gov account reflects over 120 qualifying payments on Loan 36 ( subsidized ), but the corresponding unsubsidized portion ( Loan 35 ), which shares the same consolidation date, repayment history, and employment certifications, shows significantly fewer qualifying payments and has not been forgiven. 

I have confirmed with both XXXX and XXXX that this is a single Direct Consolidation Loan. The separate tracking of PSLF counts appears inconsistent with published policy and results in unequal treatment of loan components that should be evaluated as one. 

I have submitted Employment Certification Forms covering over 130 months of qualifying public service employment, including periods of COVID forbearance, which per ED guidance [ will be ] credited toward IDR forgiveness and PSLF if employment is certified ( XXXX IDR Adjustment ). My PSLF tracker indicates over 199 eligible payment months, yet full forgiveness has not been applied. 

I currently have a PSLF reconsideration request, FOIA request, and Feedback Center case pending with FSA, but I have received no clear resolution. I respectfully request the following : 1. That FSA apply full PSLF discharge to the entire Direct Consolidation Loan, in accordance with 34 C.F.R. 685.219 and the Departments published policy ; 2. That all qualifying employment periods submitted via ECF be applied uniformly across both components of the loan ; 3. That a detailed accounting be provided showing how qualifying payment counts were determined and applied across the loan groupings.

Consumer complaint narrative:
Dear CFPB, I have federal student loans from my graduate education serviced by Nelnet. For several years, Ive been on the SAVE repayment plan. As you are aware, the SAVE plan was enacted during the Biden administration and has been subject to various legal challenges since its implementation. 

In XX/XX/XXXX, I read that the SAVE plan had been canceled. At the time, I was in the early stages of launching my own business and not in a financial position to begin repaying my loans. Based on my research ( including through XXXX ), I understood that applying for an unemployment deferment might be the best optioneven though I was actively working on starting a business. On XX/XX/XXXX, I applied for the unemployment deferment, and it was approved. 

However, by XXXX I realized that this course of action had unintended financial consequences. I contacted Nelnet and requested to be removed from the unemployment deferment, and they reinstated me on the SAVE plan effective XX/XX/XXXX. 

The issue is that when I applied for the deferment on XX/XX/XXXX, Nelnet retroactively set the start date to XX/XX/XXXX. Because interest accrues during unemployment deferment ( unlike under the SAVE plan ), they retroactively added approximately {$6000.00} in accrued interest to my account. 

I fully acknowledge that applying for the unemployment deferment was a mistake, and I certainly did not intend for it to be backdated to XX/XX/XXXX. As soon as I became aware of the financial implications, I took immediate action to correct the situation. Ive sent multiple emails and spoken to Nelnet customer service by phone, most recently on XX/XX/XXXX. 

While Nelnet was able to reinstate me on the SAVE plan, they stated they can not reverse the accrued interest, citing Department of Education policy. They also mentioned that many other borrowers have experienced the same issue, and that there is nothing they can do. 

I dont know whether the fault lies with Nelnet or the Department of Education , but it seems deeply unfair that a borrower can complete a form online andwithout clear disclosure, confirmation, or any noticeincur thousands of dollars in retroactive interest. I previously worked at a bank that issued credit, and we were constantly scrutinized to ensure compliance with fair lending practices and consumer protections. In my experience, no private lender would be allowed to apply this kind of retroactive charge without consequenceyet Nelnet and the Department of Education appear to operate above those standards. 

Please let me know what additional information you may need from me.

I never agreed to go paperless, and had I received proper mailed notices, I would have been in a better position to stay informed and avoid unnecessary penalties or credit damage. Ive also dealt with poor communication, misleading guidance, and inconsistent servicing including multiple servicer transfers where essential documentation was lost or delayed. Ive been placed in forbearance or deferment unnecessarily, and my requests for repayment plan adjustments or accurate reporting have been mishandled or ignored. The cumulative result has been long-term damage to my credit, financial well-being, and homeownership goals. Given the Department of Educations failure to protect borrower data, the mishandling of loan servicing, and the harm caused by communication failures, I am formally requesting an investigation into my account and a reconsideration of the legitimacy and enforceability of these loans. I believe loan discharge, forgiveness, or another form of relief is justified based on the misconduct and the substantial harm Ive endured. I respectfully ask that the CFPB advocate for borrowers affected by these systemic failures and hold loan servicers accountable for the barriers they continue to impose on responsible, hard-working individuals like myself.

I urge both the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) and Department of Education to investigate these violations and take corrective action consistent with federal law to protect borrowers like myself.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. I look forward to your prompt response and hope for a fair resolution.

'' XX/XX/XXXX - Second Call The issue persisted with my next payment. I called Nelnet again and received the same assurances that it was now fixed. The representative provided instructions on how to properly submit payments going forward, implying the error was somehow on my end. 
XX/XX/XXXX - Payment of {$1500.00} My auto-debit payment of {$1500.00} was processed. By my XX/XX/XXXX statement, I could see the problem was continuing : Group AC : Due date pushed to XX/XX/XXXX ( paid ahead by one year ) Group AD : Due date pushed to XX/XX/XXXX ( paid ahead by nearly one year ) Group AF : Due date pushed to XX/XX/XXXX This clearly demonstrated that despite my explicit instructions and previous calls to customer service, extra payments were still being applied to advance due dates rather than reduce principal. 
XX/XX/XXXX - Third Call After reviewing my XXXX statement and seeing the continued misapplication, I called Nelnet once again. I was told the issue had been corrected in their system. 
XX/XX/XXXX - Fourth Call After yet another payment was misapplied, I called for the fourth time. At this point, I had been dealing with this issue for over two months, calling repeatedly, and receiving the same empty promises each time.

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX of XXXX Regulations ( e-CFR ) Title XXXX Subtitle BRegulations of the Offices of the Department of Education CHAPTER VIOFFICE OF POSTSECONDARY EDUCATION, DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION PART 668STUDENT ASSISTANCE GENERAL PROVISIONS Subpart FMisrepresentation 668.71 Scope and special definitions.

34 CFR 668.71 - Scope and special definitions. 
CFR prev | next XXXX Scope and special definitions. 
( a ) If the XXXX determines that an eligible institution has engaged in substantial misrepresentation, the Secretary may ( 1 ) Revoke the eligible institution 's program participation agreement, if the institution is provisionally certified under 668.13 ( c ) ; ( 2 ) Impose limitations on the institution 's participation in the title IV, HEA programs, if the institution is provisionally certified under 668.13 ( c ) ; ( 3 ) Deny participation applications made on behalf of the institution ; or ( 4 ) Initiate a proceeding against the eligible institution under subpart G of this part.

( b ) This subpart establishes the types of activities that constitute substantial misrepresentation by an eligible institution. An eligible institution is deemed to have engaged in substantial misrepresentation when the institution itself, one of its representatives, or any ineligible institution, organization, or person with whom the eligible institution has an agreement to provide educational programs, marketing, advertising, recruiting or admissions services, makes a substantial misrepresentation about the nature of its educational program, its financial charges, or the employability of its graduates. Substantial misrepresentations are prohibited in all forms, including those made in any advertising, promotional materials, or in the marketing or sale of courses or programs of instruction offered by the institution.

( c ) The following definitions apply to this subpart : Misrepresentation. Any false, erroneous or misleading statement an eligible institution, one of its representatives, or any ineligible institution, organization, or person with whom the eligible institution has an agreement to provide educational programs, or to provide marketing, advertising, recruiting or admissions services makes directly or indirectly to a student, prospective student or any member of the public, or to an accrediting agency, to a State agency, or to the Secretary. A misleading statement includes any statement that has the likelihood or tendency to mislead under the circumstances. A misleading statement may be included in the institution 's marketing materials, website, or any other communication to students or prospective students. A statement is any communication made in writing, visually, orally, or through other means. Misrepresentation includes any statement that omits information in such a way as to make the statement false, erroneous, or misleading. Misrepresentation includes the dissemination of a student endorsement or testimonial that a student gives either under duress or because the institution required such an endorsement or testimonial to participate in a program. Misrepresentation also includes the omission of facts as defined under 668.75.

Prospective student. Any individual who has contacted an eligible institution for the purpose of requesting information about enrolling at the institution or who has been contacted directly by the institution or indirectly through advertising about enrolling at the institution.

Substantial misrepresentation. Any misrepresentation, including omission of facts as defined under 668.75, on which the person to whom it was made could reasonably be expected to rely, or has reasonably relied, to that person 's detriment.

I replied to this email asking them to retry the payment, as I had spoken with my bank. Unsure of whether or not the email was an automated server, I then looked up their number to try to call them. On their website it said they were not open on Saturdays, so I made a note to call them on Monday first thing when they were open to make sure the payment had gone through. Because I work early on Mondays and they only opened at XXXX, I had to wait until after I got out of work to call them, which was around XXXX.

I asked how this could be, as they were not even open over the weekend, and they said that because we were now in XXXX ( My payment was due by XX/XX/XXXX ), it was " too late to fix anything ''. Because I had " failed to make the payment '' before the end of the month ( my " attempt '' apparently did not count ), my loan was being sold. 

I asked to speak with someone higher up and the individual I spoke with said the same as the first. I told them I had sent an email to retry the payment, and they said this didnt matter. I asked how it was possible that they could penalize me like this, given they werent open on Saturdays to correct the problem. The agent then attempted to lie and say they were open on Saturdays and that this was clearly posted. When I told them I took screenshots of the website that clearly said they werent, they tried to backpedal and say they were open for special appointments, which I argued still wouldnt have mattered, given they would have had to have been made in advance and there was no way for me to know this was going to happen and also the knowledge of this was not made openly available to customers, so there was no way for me to know this. I offered to send them screenshots of my bank account to prove that the money was in there and it didnt get declined because I couldnt pay, and they still said this didnt matter. After I spoke with them, I called my bank and explained the situation. My bank offered to speak with them on my behalf, but this didnt matter to Sallie Mae . A previous conversation with an agent from sallie mae seemed to indicate that the company was aware of the problem and choosing not to do anything about it. After some investigation online, I found that others had reported similar situations happening with sallie mae. The complete unwillingness to do something to revert my loan status when they clearly had the ability to ( I doubt the company actually had already sold my loan after just a day ) paired with my other findings leads me to believe that this trap might be intentional or at the very least an opportunistic thing the company regularly does to profit off of customers and get off with defaulting them early to sell off debt.

Therefore, we can not remove accurate information from your credit report. From XX/XX/XXXX through XX/XX/XXXX, normally if you were to miss three monthly payments, your loans would be considered delinquent and reported to the national credit reporting agencies. However, XXXX had created a temporary on-ramp period to support you as you start or restart payments following the pandemic pause. The final on-ramp forbearance was applied to your account effective XX/XX/XXXX, to XX/XX/XXXX, preventing delinquent reporting. Your student loans were reported 90 days or more past due in XX/XX/XXXX. This reporting is accurate and can not be removed. This can include a copy of the relevant section ( s ) of your credit report highlighting the disputed reporting ; canceled checks or bank statements reflecting loan payments you believe were not applied to your account ; school enrollment information related to the loan ( s ) involved in the reporting ; an identity theft report and supporting information if you believe your loan is the result of identity theft. Consumer complaint narrative:
I am the debtor and primary borrower on certain private student loan accounts serviced by Sallie Mae. 
I filed a voluntary petition for relief under XXXX XXXX of the Bankruptcy Code. An automatic stay pursuant to 11 U.S.C. 362 ( a ) became effective in XXXX and remained in effect until XX/XX/XXXX. ( see documentation below. ) Sallie Mae received notice of my bankruptcy filing and issued electronic communications acknowledging the bankruptcy and stating that no payment was due at that time. ( see documentation below. ) During the automatic stay, Sallie Mae restricted my access to my online borrower account, preventing me from viewing loan balances, payment status, correspondence, or notices. No physical mail regarding payment obligations or account status was sent to me during this period. 
While the automatic stay was in effect, Sallie Mae unilaterally altered its internal servicing designation by treating the cosigner as the primary borrower, despite the loan contract identifying me as the primary borrower. ( see documentation below. ) During the stay, Sallie Mae contacted the cosigner by telephone and electronic communications seeking payment on the loans. These communications occurred while Sallie Mae had knowledge of the bankruptcy filing and the automatic stay. 
The cosigner did not have an online account with Sallie Mae and did not select electronic delivery preferences. Sallie Mae nevertheless relied on electronic communication preferences selected by me to justify the absence of mailed notices, while sending electronic messages stating that documents were available online. 
After termination of the automatic stay, Sallie Mae reverted the borrower and cosigner designations to their original status and asserted that the loans were delinquent due to nonpayment during the automatic stay, demanding retroactive payment for that period. ( see documentation and recorded communication below ) Sallie Mae reported the loans as XXXX or more days past due to consumer reporting agencies beginning in XXXX, including periods when the automatic stay was in effect. ( see documentation below. ) Any alleged delinquency arose solely from XXXX XXXX conduct during the automatic stay and did not exist prior to the bankruptcy filing. 
XXXX XXXX actions caused emotional distress, significant time expenditure, and damage to my credit profile, and interfered with the fresh start protections afforded by the Bankruptcy Code.

Sallie Mae had actual notice of my Chapter 7 bankruptcy and the automatic stay imposed under 11 U.S.C. 362. Notwithstanding that notice, Sallie Mae engaged in conduct that includes, but is not limited to : ( 1 ) indirect collection activity during the automatic stay by reclassifying the cosigner as the primary borrower and contacting the cosigner for payment ; ( 2 ) restricting borrower access to account information while representing that no payment was due ; ( 3 ) retroactively assessing delinquency for the stay period ; and ( 4 ) furnishing inaccurate delinquency information to consumer reporting agencies.

Anticipated Company Position and Clarification 1. Internal Policies and Procedures Anticipated Position : Sallie Mae may state that its internal policies and procedures were followed. 

Clarification : Internal policies and procedures do not supersede federal consumer protection laws applicable to private student loan lenders and servicers. Even where a company asserts compliance with its internal processes, the resulting conduct must still comply with : UDAAP prohibitions under 12 U.S.C. 5531 and 5536, FCRA accuracy and furnishing obligations under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2, and Bankruptcy Code protections, including the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. 362.

In this matter, Sallie Maes procedures resulted in the assessment of retroactive delinquency for a legally protected period, conflicting representations regarding payment obligations, and furnishing of misleading credit information. A servicing practice that produces outcomes inconsistent with federal law is not compliant, regardless of whether it aligns with internal policy. 

2. Credit Reporting Accuracy and Automation Anticipated Position : Sallie Mae may assert that credit reporting is accurate, automated, or outside its control once furnished to consumer reporting agencies.

Clarification : Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, furnishersincluding private student loan lendersare responsible for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of information they provide to consumer reporting agencies. Reporting an account as delinquent for a period during which : payment was subject to a bankruptcy automatic stay, and the borrower was informed that no payment was due, is materially misleading. The use of automated systems does not relieve a furnisher of its statutory obligation to ensure that reported information accurately reflects the legal status of the account. 

3. Cosigner Liability and Collection Activity Anticipated Position : Sallie Mae may contend that collection activity was permissible because a cosigner remained contractually liable.

Clarification : While a cosigner may remain liable under the loan contract, the conduct at issue exceeded permissible cosigner collection. During the bankruptcy period, Sallie Mae : internally altered borrower and cosigner designations without notice or authorization, relied on that alteration to maintain account activity during the automatic stay, and subsequently reversed the designation and carried forward delinquency to the primary borrower. 

This sequence reflects procedural handling that materially affected account status and post-bankruptcy delinquency, rather than ordinary cosigner collection activity, and directly contributed to retroactive payment demands and credit reporting harm. 

4. Repayment Programs and Upfront Payment Requirements Anticipated Position : Sallie Mae may state that repayment or assistance programs require financial review and an upfront payment before eligibility can be determined.

Clarification : While private student loan lenders may evaluate financial information, conditioning access to repayment options on an unspecified and undisclosed upfront payment, while refusing to disclose eligibility criteria or required amounts, raises concerns under XXXX. Withholding material information needed for a consumer to understand available options and obligations, while simultaneously demanding payment, constitutes unfair and potentially abusive servicing conduct. 

Purpose of This Clarification These clarifications are provided to ensure the CFPBs review focuses on the legal effect of XXXX XXXX servicing practices, rather than on whether internal policies were followed. The issues raised concern post-bankruptcy payment handling, credit reporting accuracy, and transparency, all of which are subject to federal consumer protection requirements for private student loan lenders.

Issue: Incorrect information on your report
Sub-issue: Account information incorrect
Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting this complaint regarding inaccurate and duplicative credit reporting related to my federal student loans, which have been serviced by Nelnet and the U.S. Department of Education.

After reviewing my credit reports, I discovered that my student loans are reporting duplicate late payments and incorrect delinquency dates across multiple tradelines. These inaccuracies appear to stem from servicer transfers and administrative changes, during which negative payment history was improperly duplicated or re-aged.

As a result, my credit file materially overstates delinquency and misrepresents my true repayment history, causing ongoing consumer harm.

. SPECIFIC PROBLEMS IDENTIFIED The issues include, but are not limited to : Duplicate late payment notations for the same periods of time appearing across multiple student loan tradelines ; Incorrect date of first delinquency and last activity dates that do not align with my actual repayment status, including periods of deferment, forbearance, income-driven repayment, or administrative transfer ; and Continued reporting of delinquency by subsequent servicers for periods that predate their servicing authority.

Federal student loans constitute a single obligation, even when transferred between servicers. Negative payment history may not be duplicated or carried forward in a manner that exaggerates delinquency.

3. WHY THIS IS A LEGAL VIOLATION ( IMPORTANT ) Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) Under 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ), consumer reporting agencies and furnishers must ensure maximum possible accuracy. Reporting that is duplicative, misleading, or that overstates delinquency violates this standard.

Under 15 U.S.C. 1681c ( a ), negative information may not be re-aged to make delinquency appear more recent than it is.

Under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ), once notified of a dispute, furnishers must conduct a reasonable investigation and correct or delete any information that can not be fully verified.

Higher Education Act Pursuant to 20 U.S.C. 1080a, federal student loan servicers are required to furnish accurate, consistent, and non-duplicative information to credit reporting agencies. Servicer transfers do not create new delinquent obligations.

Consumer Financial Protection Act ( CFPA ) Under 12 U.S.C. 5536, it is unlawful to engage in unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices, including misrepresenting loan status or furnishing information that causes consumer harm through inaccurate credit reporting.

4. HARM CAUSED The inaccurate reporting has : Artificially suppressed my credit scores ; Created barriers to obtaining mortgage approval ; Misrepresented my creditworthiness to lenders ; and Caused ongoing financial and emotional distress.

This harm is ongoing as long as the inaccurate information remains on my credit reports.

The CFPB alleged that the Trusts : " Sued consumers for debts the Trusts could not prove were owed '' Filed lawsuits although they " did not have or could not find the documentation necessary to prove either that they own the loans or that the consumer owed the debt '' The parallel to my case is exact. " Based on Information Available '' Confirms Incomplete Reporting MOHELA admits they are reporting my debt to credit bureaus " based on the information available. I am filing this complaint regarding Nelnets misleading and incomplete communication during the COVID19 payment pause and the handling of my PSLF/TEPSLF review, which together caused substantial, avoidable financial harm. This may seem like another borrower asking for an exception to a missed deadline or for special treatment on PSLF/TEPSLF. However, my request is based on the servicers misleading wording and omissions, and on objective errors in how my payments were evaluated. 

In XX/XX/XXXX Nelnet sent me a CARES Act letter explaining the COVID19 administrative forbearance on my federally owned loans. That letter stated : Although you will not be required to make monthly payments during this administrative forbearance period, payments you would have been required to make between XX/XX/XXXX, and XXXX XXXX, XXXX, will count toward loan forgiveness provided all other qualifying factors are met. The letter did not clearly explain that months in the COVID payment pause would count toward PSLF even if no payments were made. As a fulltime XXXX XXXX XXXX working mandatory overtime during the pandemic, I understood Nelnets language to mean that payment requirements were paused, but that I still needed to keep making payments in order to preserve PSLF eligibility. Acting in good faith, I continued making monthly payments throughout the COVID payment pause for 41 months, totaling {$18000.00}. 

From XX/XX/XXXX through XX/XX/XXXX, Nelnet never communicated that ( 1 ) paused months would still count as qualifying PSLF months even with no payments, and ( 2 ) payments made during the COVID19 payment pause were fully refundable if requested by the federal deadline of XX/XX/XXXX. On XX/XX/XXXX, Nelnet sent me a letter about the end of the payment pause and an administrative forbearance for XX/XX/XXXX, stating that payments would resume in XX/XX/XXXX, but did not mention the COVID refund option or the XX/XX/XXXX refund deadline, even though it was sent the same month the refund window closed. Is it reasonable for servicers like Nelnet to aggressively communicate when a payment is missed, yet stay silent about a limitedtime COVID refund right that could prevent substantial financial harm? It seems PSLF/TEPSLF borrowers like me were treated unfairly : Nelnet accepted 41 months of payments during the pause without ever clearly explaining that I did not need to pay to earn PSLF credit or that those payments were refundable. If I missed a payment today, I have no doubt Nelnet would promptly notify me, yet during the COVID pause they accepted my goodfaith payments to preserve PSLF/TEPSLF while withholding critical information about my options.

I later learned from external sources that ( 1 ) paused months did count toward PSLF even with no payments, and ( 2 ) payments made during the COVID19 pause could be refunded if requested by the deadline. When I called Nelnet to inquire about the COVID refund, I was told they could not issue a refund because the deadline had passed and was directed to submit my concerns through XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. I followed their direction and, on XX/XX/XXXX, opened Federal Student Aid Feedback Case # XXXX to request the COVIDpause reimbursement and to ask why I had never received clear and timely communication of my PSLF/TEPSLF eligibility without making payments or of the COVID refund option. In a written response dated XX/XX/XXXX, Nelnet acknowledged that I believed I had to continue making payments through the COVID19 payment pause to maintain PSLF eligibility, but denied my reimbursement request solely because the refund deadline had passed. There was no attempt at resolution and no explanation of the communication failures, just a flat denial. The XXXX XXXX XXXX closed my Feedback Case # XXXX. On XX/XX/XXXX, I formally requested my case be escalated for compliance and equity review by the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  XXXX. I have not yet received a response, so I sent an additional followup message after 90 days on XX/XX/XXXX requesting an update. The Ombudsman guidance indicates feedback and resolution within 60 days. As of today, XX/XX/XXXX, over 120 days later, I have not received any response regarding this case. How is this treatment not considered financial harm to borrowers? 

Additionally, my XX/XX/XXXX PSLF/TEPSLF application was denied. The first denial stated I was not currently eligible based on the TEPSLF 12month paymentamount test. I was advised by a XXXX phone representative to apply again, and that application was also denied. I escalated the PSLF/TEPSLF case, which was opened on XX/XX/XXXX by a XXXX phone representative ( Case # XXXX ). On XX/XX/XXXX I received a letter saying that I would need to apply for TEPSLF. Between XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX my PSLF/TEPSLF qualifying payment count changed several times, and a banner indicated that changes were being applied and accounts were being reviewed, and to expect delays. 

After another followup phone call with a XXXX representative on XX/XX/XXXX, I was told that my loans would not be eligible for PSLF/TEPSLF because they were not on an incomedriven repayment plan. On XX/XX/XXXX, I submitted an incomedriven repayment ( IDR ) application selecting the IncomeBased Repayment ( IBR ) plan to align my payments with an IDR amount. XXXX XXXX XXXX then sent a TEPSLF Missing Information Request letter dated XX/XX/XXXX, listing estimated effective forgiveness dates in XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX and requesting my income and familysize documentation. This timing shows that the renewed TEPSLF review in XX/XX/XXXX was initiated by XXXX  own processes, after earlier PSLF/TEPSLF reviews in XXXX, not by a new application from me. I provided the requested information on XX/XX/XXXX. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, I received another denial of PSLF/TEPSLF stating that We reviewed your payment history and determined that your most recent payment made and/or the payment made 12 months prior were less than the monthly incomedriven payment amount, which is not true. I have attached copies of my payments for those months ( most recent payment XX/XX/XXXX and 12 months prior XX/XX/XXXX ) to the PSLF/TEPSLF application date of XX/XX/XXXX. It appears the denial is based on incorrect paymentamount data ( showing {$64.00} ) rather than an accurate review of my actual payment history ( which shows {$420.00} ). How is there such inaccurate and constantly changing information when historical payment data are concrete? 

XXXX XXXX PSLF/TEPSLF tracking shows that I effectively reached XXXX  qualifying PSLF payments before my XX/XX/XXXX payment. By XX/XX/XXXX, that XXXX count had not changed even though I continued to make ontime payments. Since then, I have continued making payments while waiting for forgiveness to be processed. For the entire time I have been in repayment, I have consistently paid substantially above my estimated incomedriven repayment amount ; I am not asking for a refund of all amounts paid above the IDR level over the years, only for the payments that became unnecessary because of misleading COVIDpause information and PSLF/TEPSLF processing errors.

In summary, I am a longterm VA public servant who relied in good faith on Nelnets communications and XXXX  processes. Nelnets XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX letters omitted critical information about PSLF credit during the pause and about the COVID refund option and deadline, leading me to make XXXX unnecessary payments during the payment pause and miss the refund window. FSAs TEPSLF handling has required me to continue making additional payments after I met the XXXXpayment PSLF/TEPSLF threshold, and the latest TEPSLF denial appears to be based on incorrect paymentamount data. In other words, a PSLFeligible XXXX XXXX XXXX made years of qualifying payments, paid far more than her IDR requirement, and then lost access to COVID refunds and timely forgiveness because of servicer omissions and data errors, not because she ignored her obligations.

Further, continued collection activity on a loan subject to unresolved servicing errors may constitute arbitrary and capricious agency action under the Administrative Procedure Act ( 5 U.S.C. 706 ).

Please place my account into administrative forbearance while this dispute and PSLF review are pending. I request a written response within 30 days.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting this complaint regarding the servicing and credit reporting of my federal student loans by Nelnet following a federal consolidation transfer. 

My loans were transferred from XXXX to Nelnet during a consolidation process. The final written correspondence I received from XXXX stated that the loans were placed into administrative forbearance while consolidation was being processed ( XX/XX/year> ). 

After that communication, I received no notice from Nelnet indicating : that consolidation had completed, that forbearance had ended, that repayment had begun, or that a payment was due. 

I later received a credit monitoring alert indicating Nelnet had reported my loans as 120 days past due, causing a significant credit score drop. 

This was the first indication I had that Nelnet considered the loans delinquent. 

Electronic Communication Issues : When I accessed Nelnets website for the first time, I was required to create an account. 

During setup : -there was NO email address associated with the account, -I was required to enter an email address for the first time, yet -the account had already been enrolled in electronic statements and correspondence. 

-I did not provide affirmative electronic communication consent to XXXX XXXX and therefore no valid electronic consent existed to transfer to Nelnet XXXX 

Under the Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act ( E-SIGN Act, 15 U.S.C. 7001 ), required disclosures may only be delivered electronically with affirmative consumer consent. Enrolling an account in electronic correspondence without consent and without an email address on file does not meet this standard. 

Because no valid electronic consent existed, required billing statements and repayment notices should have been sent via U.S. mail. No mailed notices were received. 

Credit Reporting Concerns : Nelnet reported the loans as 120 days delinquent despite : -prior administrative forbearance status during consolidation, -lack of repayment notice, -lack of billing statements, and -lack of proper communication setup. 

This reporting appears inconsistent with the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ), which requires furnishers to provide accurate and complete information and conduct a reasonable investigation when disputes are raised. 

I submitted a written dispute to Nelnet. The response I received was a generic explanation of credit reporting policies and did not address the specific facts raised, including forbearance status, lack of notice, or electronic consent. 

Harm Experienced : As a result of this reporting : -My credit score dropped significantly. 
-My financial standing and credit access have been negatively impacted. 

Requested Resolution : I am requesting : -Immediate investigation of the delinquency reporting. 
-Removal of the 120-day delinquency from all consumer reporting agencies pending investigation. 

Confirmation of : -the date consolidation completed, -the date repayment allegedly began, -the method and date of any repayment notices sent with proof of delivery, -the basis for enrolling the account in electronic correspondence without affirmative consent. 
-Correction of any inaccurate credit reporting.

Consumer complaint narrative:
On or about XX/XX/XXXX, my federal student loan servicer, Aidvantage, sent me a letter informing me that my loans had been placed into an administrative forbearance due to the federal court injunction affecting the SAVE repayment plan. That letter contained two specific representations : First, it stated : " While you are in this forbearance no payment is required on your account and your interest rate will be set to 0 %. This means no interest will accrue while you are in the forbearance. '' Second, it committed to direct notification : " We will notify you before the forbearance comes to an end. We do not currently have a time estimate. We will then send you your next monthly billing statement at least 21 days before your next monthly payment is due. '' I relied on both of these written representations. 

According to publicly available information, the Department of Education directed that interest began accruing on SAVE administrative forbearance accounts effective XX/XX/XXXX. My account carries a total balance of {$430000.00} across 20 active loans with interest rates ranging from 3.40 % to 8.05 %. At full accrual rates, my account generates approximately {$65.00} to {$75.00} per day in interest charges. 

Despite this material change to my account terms, Aidvantage did not notify me. On XX/XX/XXXX, I conducted a thorough review of all communication channels and confirmed the following : ( 1 ) there is no message in my Aidvantage online inbox regarding the interest change ; ( 2 ) I received no email from Aidvantage about the interest resumption ; ( 3 ) I received no physical letter about the change, despite Aidvantage having previously sent the forbearance letter to my mailing address ; and ( 4 ) I received no telephone call. I first learned that interest had resumed accruing through public news reporting, not through any communication from my servicer. 

Between approximately XX/XX/XXXX, and the date I first learned of the change through news coverage, interest accrued on my {$430000.00} balance without my knowledge. Over approximately seven months of undisclosed accrual, this amounts to an estimated {$13000.00} to {$16000.00} in interest that accumulated while I reasonably relied on Aidvantage 's written representation that my interest rate was 0 % and that I would be notified before any change. 

This is not an isolated incident. In a prior CFPB complaint response, Aidvantage represented that my loans were " paid in full as of XX/XX/XXXX. '' This was inaccurate and was subsequently retracted. My account has also reflected contradictory loan status classifications, and Aidvantage has repeatedly failed to substantively respond to detailed written inquiries, instead providing form responses that do not address the specific questions raised. 

My experience is consistent with systemic failures documented by the U.S. Government Accountability Office. On XX/XX/XXXX, GAO publicly released Report GAO-26-108534, which found that in XX/XX/XXXX, the Office of Federal Student Aid stopped assessing student loan servicers on accuracy and call quality due to a 46 % reduction in staff. Before those assessments were discontinued, four of the five contracted servicers did not meet accuracy performance standards, triggering approximately {$850000.00} in financial penalties. Two servicers had record-keeping problems serious enough to receive the maximum penalty. The Department of Education 's own independent financial auditor separately reported in XX/XX/XXXX that the Department had a material weakness related to the reliability of its student loan data. The GAO specifically warned that inaccurate servicer records could result in borrowers being placed in the wrong repayment status or billed for incorrect amounts. The absence of federal oversight does not relieve Aidvantage of its obligation to honor its own written commitments to individual borrowers.

I am submitting this formal complaint regarding the improper handling of my federal student loan account while it is under active review for a Borrower Defense to Repayment claim.

To clarify - Even if your loans were already in default, once a Borrower Defense application is accepted and a forbearance is applied, that status should be honored and reflected across ALL systems. 

On XX/XX/year>, I received confirmation from the U.S. Department of Education that my loans were placed into FORBEARANCE due to my pending borrower defense application. This status is intended to provide temporary relief while my claim is under review. 

However, despite this confirmation : The status of my loans has not been updated in the online system to reflect the approved forbearance. 

My loan servicer has also failed to update the account accordingly. 

As a result, I have been informed that I am ineligible to receive financial aid due to the current status of my loans. 


This situation is both inaccurate and unjust. A borrower defense forbearance is a recognized federal protection and should not result in the denial or withholding of federal student aid. The failure to properly update my loan status is causing direct financial harm and interfering with my ability to continue my education. 


I am requesting the following immediate actions : Correction of my loan status in all systems to accurately reflect borrower defense forbearance Communication between the Department of Education and my loan servicer to ensure consistency Immediate restoration of my eligibility for federal financial aid Written confirmation once these corrections have been completed Under federal law, a loan that has been placed into administrative forbearance due to a pending Borrower Defense to Repayment application is not to be treated as actively in default for purposes of collection or borrower eligibility determinations. Pursuant to 34 C.F.R. 685.206 ( c ), the U.S. Department of Education is required to grant forbearance and suspend collection activity while a borrower defense claim is under review. Additionally, under the Higher Education Act ( 20 U.S.C. 1087e ) and related federal servicing requirements, once such relief is applied, the loan status must reflect that administrative action. Therefore, the fact that a loan was previously in default does not permit it to continue to be treated as defaulted once forbearance has been granted, and any continued classification or adverse action based on prior default status is inconsistent with federal law and regulation. 


This issue appears to be a breakdown in communication and compliance between federal systems and loan servicing entities. I expect prompt resolution, as this is impacting my education and financial standing.

My loans are under Borrower Defense review The Department of Education confirmed forbearance as of XX/XX/XXXX Any denial of aid based on outdated/default status is due to failure to update federal records I am being improperly penalized while under an active federal review. 

Thank you, XXXX

I am filing this complaint against Nelnet regarding inaccurate, inconsistent, and unlawfully reported late payment information across multiple federal student loan accounts. I have already filed complaints with the Federal Trade Commission ( FTC ), my State Attorney General, and the Federal Student Aid ( FSA ) XXXX  XXXX due to the seriousness and ongoing nature of these violations. 
The affected accounts include, but are not limited to : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Nelnet reported materially different delinquency statuses for the same accounts during the same months across XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. For example, during XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX, the same Nelnet accounts were reported as XXXX  days late with XXXX credit bureau, while being reported as paid on time, not delinquent, or not reported at all with the others. In later months, delinquency levels escalated inconsistently ( XXXX vs. XXXX late ), again differing by bureau. These reports can not all be accurate at the same time. 
In Nelnets written response, they stated that they furnish the same data to all consumer reporting agencies and claimed to have reviewed the accounts for accuracy. However, despite admitting they are the data furnisher, Nelnet failed to reconcile or correct the contradictory reporting and instead improperly instructed me to dispute the inaccuracies with the credit bureaus. The billing statements they provided are dated XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX and do not establish notice XXXX days prior to the reported delinquencies, which would have required notice in or before XX/XX/XXXX. This was not an isolated issue. Over XXXX XXXX federal student loan borrowers nationwide experienced credit reporting harm during the repayment restart and servicing transition period. Nelnets response ignores this systemic failure and relies on conclusory statements rather than evidence.

The servicers decision to place my loans into involuntary forbearance has disrupted my repayment progress and created uncertainty regarding my repayment status, interest treatment, and eligibility for forgiveness programs.

These circumstances raise serious concerns regarding potential violations of federal consumer protection standards, including : Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ) Nelnets actions may constitute an unfair or deceptive practice if borrowers are placed into involuntary forbearance without clear disclosure, explanation, or consent. Changing a borrowers repayment status without transparent communication or meaningful options may create harm by interrupting repayment progress and undermining borrower expectations regarding income-driven repayment programs.

Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) Concerns If my loan status has been reported to consumer reporting agencies in a manner that inaccurately reflects my repayment status during this involuntary forbearance, it may constitute inaccurate credit reporting. Borrowers should not face negative or misleading credit reporting outcomes as a result of administrative actions taken by a loan servicer.

Because this forbearance was not requested by me and appears to be the result of administrative or legal actions beyond my control, I respectfully request that the CFPB investigate this matter and require corrective action where appropriate.

Specifically, I request the following : A full audit and review of my loan servicing history.

Written clarification explaining why my loans were placed into involuntary administrative forbearance.

Confirmation that this period will not negatively affect my credit reporting, repayment status, or progress toward loan forgiveness programs.

Correction of any inaccurate credit reporting or payment tracking resulting from this status change.

Assurance that my SAVE plan enrollment and repayment status are being properly processed in accordance with federal student loan regulations.

Any necessary remediation if improper servicing or report
ing practices occurred.

Borrowers who make good-faith efforts to comply with federal repayment programs should not be harmed by litigation, administrative actions, or servicing decisions that are outside their control.

I appreciate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureaus assistance in reviewing this matter and ensuring that federal student loan borrowers receive fair and accurate loan servicing.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting this complaint because MOHELA, acting as the federal student loan servicer for the Department of Education, continues to report inaccurate and legally unverifiable late payment information on my credit reports despite receiving multiple disputes and formal requests for verification. 

The accounts involved in this complaint are : MOHELA / XXXX XXXX MOHELA / XXXX  XXXX MOHELA / XXXX  XXXX MOHELA / XXXX  XXXX These student loan accounts themselves are not being disputed. My complaint specifically concerns the late payment reporting associated with these accounts, which is inaccurate, inconsistent across credit bureaus, and unsupported by the documentation required under federal consumer protection laws. 

I have repeatedly notified MOHELA and the credit reporting agencies that the late payment data associated with these student loans is materially inconsistent across XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The same accounts are reporting different delinquency severities and timelines depending on the bureau reviewing the data. In some cases, the accounts show conflicting XXXX, XXXX, and XXXX late designations for the same periods of time. 

A single federal student loan can not legitimately generate multiple conflicting delinquency histories across credit bureaus. The presence of these contradictions demonstrates that the information being furnished does not meet the legal standard of maximum possible accuracy required under federal law. 

In addition to the conflicting delinquency timelines, the accounts also reflect inconsistent reporting regarding payment history, activity dates, and other servicing information. These discrepancies indicate that the information being furnished is not being verified through actual servicing records. 

Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, once a consumer disputes information, the furnisher of that information has a legal obligation to conduct a reasonable investigation using the underlying records that support the reporting. 

Furthermore, under the Fair Credit Billing Act, a reported delinquency must be supported by accurate billing records. This includes original billing statements, payment due dates, payment posting histories, and any applicable deferment or forbearance records. 

As the federal student loan servicer, MOHELA maintains the servicing records necessary to verify whether any payment was truly late. These records include billing statements, repayment schedules, servicing histories, loan status codes, deferment records, and forbearance documentation. 

Despite my requests, MOHELA has not produced the documentation required to substantiate the late payment reporting. Instead, the late payments continue to be furnished to the credit reporting agencies without providing the underlying records that would verify their accuracy. 

Without the original billing statements, repayment schedules, payment posting records, and servicing status documentation, there is no legitimate basis for continuing to report these late payments. 

In addition, the responses that have been provided appear to rely on automated system confirmations rather than an actual investigation of the loan servicing records. Automated responses or batch confirmations do not meet the legal standard for a reasonable investigation once a consumer has identified specific inaccuracies. 

The continued reporting of these late payments despite the documented inconsistencies suggests that MOHELA has not conducted a proper investigation into the accuracy of the information being furnished to the credit reporting agencies. 

The inaccurate reporting of late payments on federally serviced student loans has a significant negative impact on my credit profile and my ability to obtain credit on fair terms.

Sub-issue: High pressure sales tactics or recruiting
Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting this complaint regarding a private student loan issued by Sallie Mae, which I believe involved unfair and deceptive lending practices, compounded by a lack of adequate guidance during my college enrollment process. 

I am a first-generation college student from a single-parent household. Neither my parent nor I had any prior experience navigating higher education financing. Throughout early XXXX, after applying to the XXXX XXXX XXXX, I made repeated attempts to contact the universitys financial aid office to understand my options for scholarships, grants, or other financial assistance. Despite multiple calls, I was unable to obtain clear or actionable information and was frequently redirected without meaningful support. 

It was not until I attended in-person orientation ( after incurring travel expenses we could not afford ) that I was informed that my full out-of-state tuition balance would be due and that I had not qualified for institutional financial aid. At that point, I was told that my only remaining option to attend was to take out private student loans. This created a situation of significant stress, pressure and urgency, as I had already committed time, money, and effort toward attending the university. 

Under these circumstances, I applied for and was immediately approved for a large private loan through Sallie Mae, despite having limited financial experience and no meaningful understanding of complex loan terms. I reasonably relied on the assumption that such a loan would be structured in a way that was manageable and appropriate for a student borrower. 

Critically, I did not understand nor was it clearly explained to me in a way I could reasonably comprehend, that the loan was structured in a manner that would result in negative amortization. I believed that my required monthly payments of {$25.00} would at least cover accruing interest or reduce my balance. Instead, the loan allowed substantial unpaid interest to accrue and capitalize over time. 

As disclosed in the loan documents, more than {$19000.00} in unpaid interest was expected to accrue during the initial repayment period alone. As a result, despite making all required payments on time and never missing a payment, my loan balance has increased significantly from approximately {$41000.00} to nearly {$60000.00}. While I am still enrolled in school. 

Additionally, the loan carries a high, variable interest rate ( over 11 % at origination, with the potential to rise substantially ), further exacerbating the financial burden. The structure and terms of this loan were not adequately explained in a way that accounted for my lack of financial sophistication as a first-generation student borrower. 

Due to the financial strain and the realization that I would need to take out similarly large private loans for each remaining year of my education, I was ultimately forced to transfer to a different institution. Continuing at the XXXX XXXX XXXX would have required me to incur an unsustainable level of debt over multiple years. This decision significantly altered my educational path and was not based on academic preference, but rather on the financial hardship and risk created by the loan structure and lack of adequate guidance. 

I believe this loan was issued without proper consideration of my ability to repay and was structured in a way that is inherently harmful to borrowers, particularly those in vulnerable or inexperienced positions. I further believe that the combination of inadequate institutional guidance and the lenders approval of a high-risk loan contributed to my current financial hardship. 

I am requesting that this loan be reviewed for potential relief, including but not limited to interest reduction, balance adjustment, or discharge, based on unfair, deceptive, or predatory lending practices. 

I am prepared to provide supporting documentation, including the loan disclosure showing the accrual of unpaid interest and the resulting increase in loan balance despite consistent, on-time payments.

The conduct of the U.S. Department of Education and its contracted servicers constitutes not only administrative error, but also actionable negligence and wrongful acts under federal tort principles, including those recognized under the Federal Tort Claims Act ( FTCA ), 28 U.S.C. 1346 ( b ).

-- - Key Facts- SSA determined I became XXXX effective XX/XX/XXXX, and I remain entitled to XXXX benefits. 
- My loans entered a TPD discharge process beginning approximately XXXX. 
- I submitted required documentation during the post-discharge monitoring period, including a sworn statement dated XX/XX/XXXX, with supporting tax documentation. 
- My loans were later reinstated for alleged failure to provide documentation, which is factually incorrect. 
- Federal Student Aid records show a TPD discharge application completed on XX/XX/XXXX. 
- Later records reflect inconsistent statuses, including a closed TPD record in XXXX without explanation. 
- By XXXX, my loans were placed into default and transferred to the Default Resolution Group, with a balance exceeding {$270000.00}. 

-- - Federal Tort Liability Framework 1. Negligence ( Failure to Properly Process and Maintain Records ) Under the FTCA, the United States is liable for negligent acts of its employees acting within the scope of their duties.

The Department of Education and its agents failed to : - Properly process submitted documentation - Maintain accurate records - Apply governing regulations correctly This constitutes a breach of the duty of reasonable care in administering federal loan discharge programs.

Courts recognize that negligence arises where a duty exists, that duty is breached, and damages result. See, 350 U.S. 61 ( 1955 ).

-- - 2. Negligent Misrepresentation/ Administrative Misconduct Servicers and federal representatives provided inconsistent and conflicting information regarding the status of my loans and the basis for reinstatement.

Liability for negligent misrepresentation arises where false or misleading information is supplied in the course of official duties. See, 460 U.S. 289 ( 1983 ).

The inability of representatives to identify a valid reinstatement trigger further demonstrates systemic administrative failure.

-- - 3. Arbitrary and Capricious Action ( APA Overlay ) The reinstatement of my loans without a clear regulatory basis violates the Administrative Procedure Act.

An agency must articulate a rational basis for its decisions. See, 463 U.S. 29 ( 1983 ).

No such rational basis has been provided.

-- - 4. Procedural Due Process Violations Reinstating discharged loans without adequate notice or explanation constitutes deprivation of a property interest without due process.

See, 424 U.S. 319 ( 1976 ).

-- - 5. Wrongful Collection Activity The continued collection of debt that has been dischargedor should have been dischargedconstitutes improper government action.

Courts recognize that the government may be liable when it wrongfully enforces obligations not legally owed. See, 518 U.S. 839 ( 1996 ) ( government liability for improper enforcement of obligations ).

Preservation of all records related to this matter for potential legal review -- - Notice of Potential Federal Tort Claim This complaint also serves as notice that the conduct described herein may form the basis of a claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act.

If not resolved administratively, I intend to pursue all available legal remedies, including claims for negligence, administrative misconduct, and improper collection of debt.

I am writing to formally rebut MOHELAs most recent explanation regarding the approximately {$27000.00} increase in my federal student loan balance during the XXXX XXXX administrative forbearance period. 
After XXXX  months of continuous attempts to obtain a clear and accurate accounting, MOHELA has now provided an explanation that is not only unsupported by documentation but also inconsistent with the fundamental mechanics of federal student loan interest accrual and servicing practices. 
I. Core Issue This correspondence focuses exclusively on one issue : The unexplained addition of approximately {$27000.00} to my loan balance between XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX during a period in which my loans were subject to 0.0 % interest administrative forbearance under the XXXX XXXX. 
There were : No new loan disbursements, and No valid mechanism for interest accrual Under these conditions, the loan balance should have remained static, as it did during the XXXX administrative forbearance period. 

II. Summary of MOHELAs Explanation MOHELA now asserts that : Interest was incorrectly capitalized ( ~ {$25000.00} ) ; Their system calculates hypothetical interest and reduces it during 0 % periods ; Overlapping forbearance periods caused negative accrued interest ; This negative interest was later corrected, resulting in balance adjustments.

III. Technical Rebuttal This explanation is not credible for the following reasons : 1. Negative Interest Can not Exist in Federal Student Loan Accounting Under federal loan servicing rules : Interest may accrue ( positive ), or Be waived/subsidized ( effectively zero ) It can not become negative. 
If an internal system over-applies an interest reduction, the correct outcome is : Interest = {$0.00} not the creation of a borrower liability. 
There is no statutory or regulatory authority permitting a servicer to : Generate a negative interest condition, and Retroactively charge the borrower to correct it 2. 0.0 % Interest Means No AccrualNot Reversible Accrual MOHELAs claim that their system : calculates interest that would have accrued and reduces it is inconsistent with how 0 % interest is applied. 
Under a valid 0.0 % interest forbearance : Interest does not accrue at all It is not : o Accrued and then reversed o Simulated and adjusted This distinction is critical. Their explanation reflects a hypothetical accounting construct, not actual loan behavior.

3. Overlapping Forbearance Periods Can not Generate Debt Even if administrative overlaps occurred : The maximum impact would be over-suppression of interest to zero It can not : Produce a deficit Justify a retroactive charge Generate a {$27000.00} balance increase 4. Timing of the Alleged Correction Is Not Credible MOHELA claims this issue resulted in : A capitalization event on XX/XX/XXXX However : The relevant forbearance periods occurred in XXXX The adjustment occurred nearly XXXX XXXX  later This delay is inconsistent with legitimate servicing corrections and raises serious concerns regarding : Retroactive account reconstruction Post hoc justification of balance changes 5. Admission of Servicing Error Without Proper Remediation MOHELA explicitly states : interest was incorrectly capitalized This is an admission of a servicing error. 
However, instead of restoring the account to its correct pre-error state, MOHELA : Introduces an unverified negative interest correction mechanism Fails to reconcile the resulting balance This does not constitute remediationit represents replacement of one unsupported adjustment with another.

6. Absence of Required Supporting Documentation Despite repeated requests, MOHELA has failed to provide : A complete, itemized loan transaction history Daily interest accrual logs Any record showing a negative interest condition Calculation methodology supporting the {$27000.00} adjustment Audit logs or system-generated correction records Without this documentation, their explanation is non-verifiable and insufficient. 

IV. Formal Position Based on the above, MOHELAs explanation : Does not align with federal loan servicing principles Is unsupported by auditable financial records Fails to justify the {$27000.00} balance increase Accordingly, the balance adjustment remains formally disputed in full.

I believe SoFi has engaged in deceptive and misleading disclosure practices regarding the application of a XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX discount to my interest rate, and has breached the material representations it made to me prior to and at the time of loan origination. 

I refinanced my student loans with SoFi through the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX program, which is available to XXXX  of SoFi 's XXXX XXXX  companies. At the time I applied, the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX website described the XXXX  discount as follows : " XXXX  % rate discount for refinancing your student loan : Terms and conditions apply. Offer good for new student loan refinancing customers only and subject to lender approval. To receive the offer, you must : ( 1 ) register and/or apply through this landing page/your SoFi XXXX XXXX Dashboard or Benefits Portal ; ( 2 ) complete a loan application with SoFi within 90 days of your application submit date ; ( 3 ) and meet SoFi 's underwriting criteria XXXX Once conditions are met and the loan has been disbursed, the interest rate shown in the Final Disclosure Statement will include an additional XXXX  % rate discount because of your involvement with a SoFi XXXX  company at the time of loan origination. '' This language is unambiguous : SoFi represented that the XXXX  % XXXX  discount would be reflected as an additional discount in the Final Disclosure Statement, applied after disbursement of the loan. I satisfied all of the stated conditions for receiving this discount. 

I signed a document entitled " SOFI BANK, N.A. REFI EDUCATION LOAN FIXED RATE APPROVAL DISCLOSURE '' ( the " Disclosure '' ). The Disclosure stated that the initial interest rate without discount would be XXXX  %. The Disclosure further stated that the interest rate " does not reflect qualifying discounts, such as Autopay Discount and SoFi Plus Discount. '' It did not indicate that the corporate partner discount had already been factored into the stated rate, nor did it disclose that the corporate discount was not a " qualifying discount '' for purposes of that disclosure. 

By using the phrase " such as '' when listing qualifying discounts, the Disclosure impliedbut did not excludethe existence of additional qualifying discounts, including the corporate partner discount. I reasonably understood, based on SoFi 's explicit written representations on its SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX website, that the corporate discount would be applied and separately reflected in a Final Disclosure Statement following disbursement. No such Final Disclosure Statement reflecting the additional XXXX  % discount was ever provided. 

Additionally, the Disclosure 's Reference Notes stated : " From time to time, you might be eligible for discounts and/or interest rate deductions offered by SoFi. Please refer to the terms for such offers located on the SoFi website. '' This language directly directed me to SoFi 's website terms the very terms that represented the corporate discount would be applied as an additional post-disbursement reduction. 

Once the loan was dispersed, I called SoFi to ask why my rate shown was XXXX  % and asked when the .XXXX  % corporate discount would be applied. I was then told by customer service that it had already been applied so I decided to press the issue out of confusion. When I escalated the issue with SoFi, a Resolution Specialist responded that : 1. The corporate discount had already been applied during the application process and was embedded in the XXXX  % rate shown in my Disclosure ( i.e., the initial rate before the XXXX discount was allegedly XXXX  % ) ; XXXX. The XXXX  discount is " permanent '' and therefore is not disclosed separately in the loan documents and is given at some point in the application process that I would not have any record of ; 3. The terms I cited were from a source dated XX/XX/year> and that SoFi reserves the right to change or terminate its discount program. 

I find this response inadequate and misleading for the following reasons : I can not find any record of a corporate discount being disclosed. Neither my Disclosure nor any other loan document I received identified the corporate discount, its amount, or the fact that it had been applied. If the corporate discount was embedded in the XXXX  % rate, SoFi was obligated to disclose it as such ( and even if they did disclose it in the application process, there should be some kind of record of this application in the documentation I signed which there was not ). Concealing a discount within a stated rate is not a transparent or adequate disclosure, particularly where SoFi 's own written materials represented it would be separately identified in a Final Disclosure Statement.

SoFi 's terms expressly stated the discount would be applied after disbursement. The plain language of SoFi 's SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX terms states the discount would appear in the Final Disclosure Statement after disbursement not before. SoFi can not now retroactively recharacterize the discount as having been applied during the application stage. This is inconsistent with its own representations. 

The argument that the terms were outdated is unavailing. SoFi did not notify me prior to or at the time of my loan application that the terms on the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX website were outdated, inapplicable, or had been superseded. I relied in good faith on the representations set out on SoFi 's own platform when deciding to refinance through the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX program. 

SoFi has failed to respond to my follow-up request. After receiving SoFi 's initial response, I replied requesting that SoFi apply the disputed XXXX  % discount to my ongoing interest rate on both a going-forward and retroactive basis. SoFi did not respond to this request. I have also made multiple phone calls to SoFi 's customer service, and representatives have told me there is nothing they can do to help. 

As a direct result of SoFi 's failure to properly apply the XXXX  % corporate discount as represented : 1. I am paying an interest rate of XXXX % rather than the XXXX  % I am entitled to under SoFi 's own terms.

2. I have been and continue to be overcharged interest on the outstanding principal balance of my loan.

3. I relied on SoFi 's material representations in entering into this loan and would not have done so on the same terms had SoFi 's representations been accurate and complete. 

While XXXX % may appear to be a modest figure in isolation, when applied to a loan balance over the full term of the loan, it represents a meaningful financial harm to me. I also have reason to believe that other SoFi borrowers who refinanced through the SoFi XXXX XXXXXXXX program may be in the same situation, having similarly relied on SoFi 's representations without receiving the benefit of the promised discount.

My payment was {$170.00} per month. From XXXX to XXXX, I properly applied for recertification under the PAYE plan, and was recertified. My payment remained {$170.00} per month throughout that period. I have never missed a payment and, as far as I can recall, have never made a late payment. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, I received a letter from my loan servicer, Mohela, regarding my XXXX application for recertification. This letter stated that my application for recertification had not been approved. I have attached this letter to this complaint ( XXXX XXXX XXXX Mohela Letter - IDR Request Denied ). Without this IDR plan, my minimum payment would have increased to approximately {$1700.00} per month. I was a remain completely financially incapable of making a month payment of that amount. Either that same day or in the days immediately following, I contacted Mohela by phone, requesting more information about the denial, and I was informed that, due to the recent Big, Beautiful Bill, borrowers were required to prove a financial hardship to qualify for the PAYE plan. Despite living paycheck to paycheck, I was told that I did not qualify for a financial hardship. However, the Mohela representative encouraged me to apply for an Income-Based Repayment Plan ( IBR ). She said that this plan used a similar calculation for payments as the PAYE plan, and seemed optimistic that my payment would remain the same as they were. Unfortunately, I do not recall the name of the Mohela representative I spoke with.

Thereafter, I applied for the IBR plan as suggested by the Mohela representative. During the application process, the XXXX XXXX XXXX website provided an estimate of my new monthly payment under the IBR plan, estimating that my new payment would be {$780.00} per month. This would represent a 460 % increase from my previous payment of {$170.00} per month. Despite this estimate, I relied on the representation made by the Mohela representative that my payment would be the same as it had been under the PAYE plan, and applied for the IBR plan. While I was relying on the representation made by Mohela, I also knew that I could not afford to meet the Standard Repayment Plan payment of approximately {$1700.00} per month, and recognized that I had no choice but to apply for the IBR plan even if the payment would increase to {$780.00} per month. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, I received a letter from Mohela stating that my application for the IBR plan was accepted. This letter stated that my new monthly payment would be {$780.00} per month. I have attached that letter to this complaint ( XXXX XXXX XXXX Mohela Letter 1 - New Monthly Payment ). 

I was extremely disheartened by the fact that my payment had not remained the same and had increased by 460 %. While I was aware that this was possible, I remained hopeful based on Mohelas representation that my payment would likely stay the same as it was under the PAYE plan. However, as noted previously, I had no choice but to accept this increased payment, as remaining on a Standard Repayment Plan was not financially possible. 

Also on XX/XX/XXXX, after receiving the letter with my new payment, I received a second letter from Mohela, providing details about the schedule of my loan repayment. Much to my surprise, this letter stated that my payment would be {$780.00} per month for the next 12 months, and then increase again to {$990.00} per month. {$990.00} per month would reflect a 584 % increase in my previous minimum payment amount over the course of one year. No explanation was provided for why my payments were set to increase after 12 months, and this increase in my payment amount did not appear to be tied to my income. I have attached that letter to this complaint ( XXXX XXXX XXXX Mohela Letter 2 - Repayment Schedule ).

This 584 % increase in my payment amount is unconscionable. I have a two and a half year old daughter and am the primary income-earner for her and my wife. Like many other Americans, I also have to make payments for my mortgage, my wifes car loan, and credit card debt. This is taking place in an environment of increasing inflation and rapidly rising prices across the economy. I am not financially capable of making these payments.

Mohela is also engaging in predatory practices. As mentioned, I had no choice but to apply for this new plan, because, otherwise, my minimum payment would have increased to {$1700.00} per month, which, as stated above, I am not financially capable of making. In applying for this plan, I relied on the representations made by Mohela that my payment would likely remain the same as it was.
